clue.text: "Club" singer taking over, that surprises me!

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: 'By George!' is an old exclamation of surprise
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Someone at a nightclub gasps as a singer seizes the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'Club' point to Culture Club, the 1980s band fronted by BOY GEORGE; 'By George!' just needs an O slipped in after the B.
explanation.definitionFit: Boy George was the lead vocalist of the pop band Culture Club, famous for Karma Chameleon.

clue.text: Fashionable young thing, Kay Short

indicators.note: to be short of something is to lack it, so that letter is missing

parts.note: a chick is a young bird, or slangily a young woman
Kay is the spoken name of the letter K

explanation.surface: A stylish young woman called Kay Short is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kay Short' reads as a person's name, but Kay is the letter K and Short says the chick goes without it.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic describes something elegant and stylish, a direct synonym for being in fashion.

clue.text: Disorderly non-members knocking out some poor guy in changing room

indicators.note: disorderly means out of order, so the letters of non-members are scrambled
knocking out says the letters of the second word are taken out of the first before the rest are rearranged
poor means in bad shape, so the word some is itself jumbled, and only its letters matter

explanation.surface: Rowdy outsiders beat up some unlucky man in a changing room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' says the word removed need not appear in order: 'knocking out' takes its four letters from scattered places. Mr Benn, a bowler-hatted children's TV cartoon character from the 1970s, steps into a fancy-dress shop's changing room before each adventure.
explanation.definitionFit: In each episode the cartoon hero enters a costume shop's fitting room and emerges into an adventure matching the outfit he tried on.

clue.text: Out of hospital, the reason to admit one's soft, weak and feeble

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so pieces are placed inside another
something out of a place has left it, so that letter goes missing

parts.note: why asks for a reason
H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital
one's read as 'one is', I'M
p (piano) is the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A patient discharged from hospital wonders aloud why they feel so feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: Lose the H from WHY to leave W_Y, then put I'M and P in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Wimpy means lacking strength or courage, so it matches feeble and weak as a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Perhaps Clementine, Charlotte and Lauryn will have to share a cell

indicators.text: will have to share a cell
indicators.note: sharing a cell means two occupants use one grid square, so one overlapping letter is dropped

parts.note: Charlotte Church is a Welsh singer
Lauryn Hill is an American singer and rapper

explanation.surface: Three women are told they must be locked up together in one prison cell.
explanation.walkthrough: The surnames end and begin with the same H, which serves both; the cell is a grid square rather than a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Clementine was the wife of Winston, so her surname makes her one example of the family name.

clue.text: Band sacked woman missing vocal elements in hotspots

indicators.note: sacked, in the sense of plundered and laid waste, says the letters are thrown into disorder
missing means the word woman goes without the letters named next

parts.note: vowels are the voiced letters of a word; here the vowels of woman, O and A

explanation.surface: A band has fired a female member who keeps missing her notes at hot venues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing vocal elements' strips the vowels from WOMAN to leave WMN, which joins IN and HOTSPOTS for 'sacked' to rearrange. The 1980s band took its name from the bowler-hatted detectives in Tintin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thompson Twins were a British new wave pop group of the 1980s, so a musical group.

clue.text: Mistake Wayne's inspiration for clash of heads? This is on Riddler

indicators.note: for a clash of the two words swaps something between them, so the mistake word gives up its opening letter for the other's

parts.note: a howler is a glaring mistake

indicators.note: heads are the opening letters, here the ones the two words trade

parts.note: Bruce Wayne took the bat as the inspiration for his Batman costume

explanation.surface: A comic-book fan blames a blunder in Batman lore for a head-on collision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clash of heads' swaps the first letters of HOWLER and BAT, the H and the B. The Riddler, a Batman villain, is often drawn wearing this hat, which is the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowler hat is a hard round felt hat, and the Riddler often wears one in the Batman comics.

clue.text: See 17
One of two possibly having left this place unclad

indicators.note: unclad means stripped of clothing, so the phrase loses its outer letters at each end

parts.note: someone who has left this place is not here

explanation.surface: One of a pair has apparently gone off naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having left this place' gives NOT HERE, and 'unclad' strips its first and last letters. The definition is fair because the answer completes 'one or the other'.
explanation.definitionFit: Of a pair, 'the other' is the second one, the alternative to the first.

clue.text: In that region, Hungary lies to the west

indicators.note: in an across answer west is the left, so this piece is written first

parts.note: a place that lies somewhere is there
H is the international vehicle code for Hungary

explanation.surface: A geography note: in that part of Europe, Hungary sits to the west.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as 'Hungary: IS lies to the west of it'; 'region' points to approximation, as in 'about ten-ish'.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix or word '-ish' means roughly or approximately, so 'in that region' of a number or time.

clue.text: In both directions I see a commotion

indicators.note: both directions means backwards as well as forwards, so a copy is turned around

parts.note: 'Oh, I see' — the exclamation of understanding, here taken backwards
the same exclamation again, this time forwards
taken as written

explanation.surface: Looking left and right, someone spots a disturbance.
explanation.walkthrough: OH is written backwards and then forwards, then A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-ha is a noisy fuss or uproar, a colloquial synonym for commotion.

clue.text: Cool, not having old pile sell at a low price

indicators.note: not having something means lacking it, so those letters are removed

parts.note: to cool is to go cold
taken as written
a heap is a pile

explanation.surface: Something trendy, but not the crumbling old mansion, being sold off cheaply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' looks like an adjective meaning trendy but is the verb; 'old pile' tempts as a stately home, yet old and pile do separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods that go cheap are sold for very little money, an everyday idiom for a low sale price.

clue.text: Hit on the fact that the spirit of the Caribbean was flowing freely

parts.note: rum is distilled from Caribbean sugar cane
a wound that bled had blood flowing from it

explanation.surface: Someone realises that the rum was flowing generously at a Caribbean party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowing freely' tempts toward drink, but it is about blood; rumbled is British slang for found out.
explanation.definitionFit: To rumble someone or something is informal British for discovering the truth, seeing through a deception.

clue.text: Henry working with wrapping present

indicators.note: wrapping means the working and with words are folded around the Henry letter

parts.note: on means working or functioning, as a switched-on machine is
and means with, joining things together
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Henry is busy wrapping a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as Henry wrapping a present, but the wordplay runs the other way: 'working with' does the wrapping, and Henry is what gets wrapped.
explanation.definitionFit: On hand means available or nearby, so in attendance, which is a sense of present.

clue.text: See 7
E.g. Menace, Destroyer and Governess, finally on the heels of optimistic bunch?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: nicknames of the quizzers on the TV show The Chase

definitions.text: finally on the heels of optimistic bunch
definitions.meaning: second meaning: pursuers who hope at last to catch up with those ahead

explanation.walkthrough: The Chase is a British TV quiz in which contestants race a resident expert with a nickname such as the Menace, the Destroyer or the Governess.
explanation.definitionFit: The show's experts are called by that title, and anyone pursuing in hope of catching up does the same job.

clue.text: Universal parts are light, just to promote 50 actors

indicators.note: to part something is to split it open, so the first piece goes into a gap in the second
to promote is to move up, and in a down answer up means earlier, so a letter leaves its spot for the top

parts.note: to light on something is to land on it
hardly means only just
L is the Roman numeral for 50
taken as written
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing

explanation.surface: A Hollywood studio is handing out light roles to promote fifty actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Universal' is the studio in the surface; build AURE, LAND and HARDLY, then lift the L of HARDLY up to the top of the column.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy were the famous comedy double act of early Hollywood films.

clue.text: Ladies and gents got ready to strike Avenger

parts.note: the Ladies and the Gents are public toilets, and john is slang for a toilet
a golfer who teed up set the ball ready to hit

explanation.surface: Men and women prepare to strike back at a vengeful foe.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ladies and the Gents are British names for public toilets; John Steed was the bowler-hatted agent of the 1960s TV series The Avengers.
explanation.definitionFit: Steed was the leading character of the British spy show, so he is literally one of its title figures.

clue.text: Enjoyable German channel

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the German word for good
second meaning: a narrow passage of water, or the alimentary canal

explanation.walkthrough: 'German channel' sounds like a TV station; instead the first two words are one meaning and the last another.
explanation.definitionFit: A gut is a narrow strait or watercourse, and also the body's digestive canal.

clue.text: Love is returned by crack director

parts.note: to chap is to crack, as skin does in the cold

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so it is written backwards

parts.note: love is a score of zero in tennis

explanation.surface: A first-rate film director wins back the affection of his audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crack' reads as an adjective meaning expert, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Chaplin directed his own silent films such as Modern Times as well as starring in them.

clue.text: Thick skin envelops cubic body mass

indicators.note: to envelop is to wrap around, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a callus is a patch of hardened skin
cu is the standard abbreviation for cubic, as in cu ft

explanation.surface: A hard skin forms around a solid cube-shaped lump in the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body mass' sounds like a weight measurement, but it is a medical term for a hard lump; 'cubic' is the abbreviation seen in cu ft.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine a calculus is a hard stone formed in an organ, such as a kidney stone.

clue.text: International event; international lingo

parts.note: I is a standard abbreviation for international
a do is a party or social event

explanation.surface: A global gathering is described alongside the shared tongue its delegates speak.
explanation.walkthrough: Ido is a constructed language developed from Esperanto in 1907.
explanation.definitionFit: Ido was built as a universal auxiliary language for speakers of different nations to share.

clue.text: See 23
As a joke, eyes kissing when moving south east

indicators.note: east is the right-hand end of an across answer, so this letter is taken from its place and put last

parts.note: oscular means relating to kissing
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Eyes meet playfully as two people kiss and head off south-east together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'south east' reads as a compass bearing, but south is S and east says where it goes: to the end of OSCULAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Oculars is a humorous or facetious term for the eyes, hence the jocular label in the clue.

clue.text: Macabre hairy relative practisin' sex in bed

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so these pieces go into another

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
practising is using, here with the G dropped as the apostrophe shows
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: A ghoulish, shaggy family member is caught in bed getting up to no good.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped G in 'practisin'' tells you to drop it from USING too; Cousin Itt is the hair-covered relative in The Addams Family.
explanation.definitionFit: The Addams Family are a ghoulish clan, and Itt is the cousin made entirely of floor-length hair.

clue.text: Secured additional part of Greater Manchester

parts.note: to bolt is to secure a door
on means further or in addition, as in 'and so on'

explanation.surface: An extra piece is fixed in place, like a bolt-on added to a machine.
explanation.walkthrough: Greater Manchester is a metropolitan county in north-west England made up of several towns.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolton is a large town that forms one of the ten boroughs of that English metropolitan county.

clue.text: Some casual work retiring PM takes in Dutch Department

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the name is written backwards
to take in is to receive inside, so pieces go into a gap

parts.note: BoJo is the nickname of Boris Johnson, the British Prime Minister
D is an abbreviation for Dutch
D is an abbreviation for department

explanation.surface: An outgoing prime minister picks up a bit of casual work in a Dutch ministry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' fits Boris Johnson stepping down, but it is also the reversal signal; the two Ds sit after the first O.
explanation.definitionFit: An odd job is a single piece of casual or occasional work, such as a small household repair.

clue.text: A division secretly devising gadgets to clean up Muslim dress

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means read from the bottom, so the whole is reversed

parts.note: taken as written
Q Branch devises gadgets for the spies in the James Bond stories
to rub something can clean it

explanation.surface: A secret department invents gadgets for washing a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: Q is the gadget-maker of the James Bond films; 'clean up' looks like one phrase but up reverses everything before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A burqa is the full-body outer garment worn by some Muslim women, covering head and face.

clue.text: See 6
Remarkable turnout, so unable to offer seconds

indicators.note: seconds here means every second letter, so the even-placed letters are kept

parts.note: the even-numbered letters of these three words

explanation.surface: An event draws a big crowd, so the kitchen cannot serve second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seconds' looks like second helpings of food, but it asks for the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unusual is out of the ordinary and so worth remarking on, a close synonym.

clue.text: Player in the auditorium you've no reason to question

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so what is heard matters, not what is written

parts.note: said as a rhetorical question: there is no reason for suspicion

explanation.surface: An actor on stage seems so convincing the audience has no cause for suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests an actor in the auditorium, but this is a position in American football, the receiver who lines up wide.
explanation.definitionFit: In American football a wideout, or wide receiver, is an offensive player positioned near the sideline to catch passes.

clue.text: Into getting hammered, overdoing the amber nectar?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: engaged with or keen on something

definitions.text: getting hammered, overdoing the amber nectar
definitions.meaning: second meaning: British slang for drinking heavily

explanation.walkthrough: Amber nectar is beer, from an Australian lager advert; being 'on it' is British slang for a drinking session.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both actively dealing with something and being on a heavy drinking binge.

clue.text: Parisian who turned up recording device

parts.note: qui is French for who

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so its letters are written backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Frenchman shows up with a tape recorder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recording device' suggests electronics, but this is the Inca system of knotted cords used to keep records.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas kept accounts and census data on knotted strings, so it was literally a device for recording.

clue.text: Religious party to join union

indicators.note: to be party to something is to be involved in it, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A church faction decides to sign up to a trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Religious party' reads as one phrase, a church faction, but the definition is the single word: a religious is a member of an order.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, a religious is a person bound by monastic vows, and a nun is one such woman.

clue.text: Nothing particularly good in reserve

parts.note: O looks like zero
nice means pleasant, and in an older sense precise or particular

explanation.surface: Nothing special is being held back for later.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice once meant fastidious or particular, which helps explain the pairing.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans put on ice are shelved and kept for later use, an idiom for being held back.
